title: The Gentleman Conjuror
description: Robert-Houdin's rules for a believable performer, and a card trick played straight
tryIt: Practise the Gentleman's Peek five times alone with a deck, then perform it for one person in ordinary clothes, with one short true-sounding story and no jokes.

concepts.title: How it works: an actor playing a magician
concepts.contentHtml:
Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin was born in Blois on 6 December 1805, the son of a watchmaker, and he learned to work with his hands on clocks and mechanical toys. On 3 July 1845 he opened a tiny theatre at the Palais Royal in Paris and invited the public to his "fantastic soirées". Cambridge University Press, which reissues his Secrets of Conjuring and Magic (first published in 1868), describes him as often called the father of modern conjuring.1

What did he change? Mostly the person doing the tricks. In his memoirs he says he avoided any eccentric costume and wore the ordinary evening dress of polite society, because bizarre clothes only cast disfavour on the wearer. He also set himself a rule he never broke: to make no puns or play upon words, and never to permit myself to be guilty of a mystification, even were I sure of gaining the greatest success.2 He wanted experiments, as he put it, divested of all charlatanism.

A famous line is credited to him: a conjuror is an actor playing the part of a magician. We could not check its exact wording against a scan of the 1868 book, so treat the words as reported, not confirmed. The idea, though, is plain in his own rules. The character is part of the performance, and the character he chose was a courteous, truthful gentleman who happens to have a knack.

That is the first lesson of this course's last skill: you are not claiming powers, you are playing someone with a trick up his sleeve. Say "let me try something", never "I can read minds". An audience forgives a trick that goes wrong far more readily than a lie.

concepts.title: The method: the Gentleman's Peek
concepts.contentHtml:
This is the Gentleman's Peek, Robert-Houdin's rule in card form: nobody takes a card out, shows a card or signs anything; they only look at one. Example cards: the 6♦ is your key and the J♠ is their card.

  1. Glimpse. Square the deck face down and tip the inner end up for a second as you tidy it. Read the bottom card: the 6♦. (They see a person tidying.)
  2. Lift. Ask them to lift off about half the deck from the top and hold it. Call it U. Your cards are L, with the 6♦ at the bottom.
  3. Peek. Ask them to look at the top card of the packet in their hands, remember it, and put the packet on the table. It is the J♠, but you never see it.
  4. Drop. Say "let me keep things tidy" and drop L squarely on U. The 6♦ now lies directly on their J♠.
  5. Cuts. They cut the deck and complete the cut, as often as they like. Neighbours stay neighbours.
  6. Find. Deal face up into a heap, telling your story. When the 6♦ lands, put the next card face down to one side, ask them to name their card, and turn it over.

Patter in Robert-Houdin's spirit: dress normally, speak plainly and give the trick a small true story ("I learned this from a book older than my grandmother"). Mistakes to avoid: asking for the bottom card of their packet (it would be the wrong end, away from the key), shuffling after step 4, and letting your glimpse look like a glimpse.

concepts.title: Myth check: Houdini's hero
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Houdini named himself after his hero Robert-Houdin and admired him to the end.
Reality He did take the name in admiration, but in 1908 he published The Unmasking of Robert-Houdin, which calls his hero a pretender.

Harry Houdini tells the first half himself. When he needed a stage-name, a fellow-player suggested adding the letter "i" to Houdin's name, meaning "like Houdin" in French. He adopted it with enthusiasm and wrote that he asked nothing more of life than to become in my profession1 "like Robert-Houdin". By then he had re-read the master's works until he could recite passages from memory.

Wait, really? The same man later researched the history of conjuring and reported "only bitterest disappointment". In The Unmasking he says that, stripped of his self-woven veil of romance, Robert-Houdin stood forth as a mere pretender,2 a man who waxed great on the brainwork of others. He also claimed that the famous memoirs were really written by a Parisian journalist. Those are Houdini's charges, made by a man with his own legend to protect. This course has not checked each one, so treat them as one magician's verdict on another.

The lesson for your own performing: even heroes disagree about each other, and a reputation is partly a story that someone chose to tell. Robert-Houdin's costume rules, at least, are in his own words and still work.

title: The Book With No Author
description: Erdnase's 1902 treatise, the unsolved hunt for its author, and a thought-of card with a break
tryIt: Practise holding a little-finger break on the deck ten times, then perform the thought-of card for one person without ever saying you can read minds.

concepts.title: How it works: a book that hid its author
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1902 a book appeared in Chicago whose title page reads Artifice, Ruse and Subterfuge at the Card Table, "by S. W. Erdnase", with over one hundred drawings from life by M. D. Smith. It became better known as The Expert at the Card Table. It was self-published, and in the words of one history of the hunt for its author, it has "never gone out of print". Dai Vernon, who first read it as a boy, could still quote it from memory at 88.

Who was S. W. Erdnase? The most popular theory is that the name is E. S. Andrews backwards. In 1946 the writer and magician Martin Gardner found the Chicago artist Marshall D. Smith, who remembered meeting the author once, 44 years earlier, and Gardner came to believe Erdnase was Milton Franklin Andrews, a cardsharp who died in 1905. Sceptics point to mismatches in Smith's memory and in writing style. Other suspects have included a railway agent, Edwin Summer Andrews, and a mining engineer, Wilbur Edgerton Sanders.

The article we read, from 2001, says Vernon never did determine the true identity of the author.1 As far as this course knows, no candidate has convinced everyone since; if you want the latest, look for recent research.

How do we know any of it? The evidence is thin: the book itself, an artist's memory of one meeting, a publisher's reported remark and old public records such as marriage licences. That is why the hunt has lasted so long.

The introduction explains the book's plan. The first part reviews advantages taken at the card table; part two "describes the sleights employed in conjuring and many very interesting card tricks". This course treats the first part as history only. Everything you learn here comes from the second.

concepts.title: The method: a thought-of card with a break
concepts.contentHtml:
Erdnase had a sharp eye for performance. In his chapter of card tricks he writes that the simplest sleight can become an astonishing trick if it is well "rigged up" with plausible patter, and that the address and patter of the performer will count as much if not more than his skill in manipulation.1

He also lists ways to find a card a spectator only thinks of. Here is a modern handling of one of them: let them cut off a packet and look at its bottom card, take the packet back "holding a break at the location". The break is a gap you hold with the tip of your little finger. Example: they see the 4♠.

  1. Offer. Hold the deck face down. Ask them to cut off a packet (P), look at the bottom card of it without showing you, and remember it.
  2. Take back. Thank them, take P and drop it on the cards in your left hand (R). As it lands, your left little finger tip slips into the gap at the inner right corner, between P and R. Hold it lightly.
  3. Cut at the break. Say "let me bury it". Lift everything above the gap (P) and put it under R. The 4♠ is now the bottom card.
  4. Glimpse. Square the deck, tipping the inner end for a moment: the 4♠.
  5. Reveal. Give clues as theatre ("a dark suit... a low card...") and then name the card. They never see how you found it.

The break is the new skill: practise until the finger holds a gap of a few millimetres without the hand looking tense. Mistakes: pressing the gap too wide, glancing at your hand, or claiming to read minds. You are performing a trick, so keep the clues playful.

concepts.title: Myth check: a cheat's bible
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Erdnase's book was the cheat's bible, studied by every sharper.
Reality According to a casino security chief, very few card cheats have ever read it, and it has influenced magicians far more.

Ron Conley, who oversees security at a California casino, told American Heritage that in 35 years around "card thieves" he had found "very few" of them had read Erdnase. The magazine's summary: the book seems to have exerted a far greater influence on card magicians than on card cheats.1 Dai Vernon, for one, called it clearer than anything else on how to perform a card move.

Card cheating has a long history, and one famous conjuror wrote about it to warn the honest. Robert-Houdin published The Sharper Detected and Exposed and says of the tricks he described that he collected them "one by one, from sharpers" at some risk, because sharpers do not willingly part with the arts on which they depend for their livelihood.2 He ends his memoirs' account with advice never to sit down but with persons "whose honor is unimpeachable".

Erdnase himself explains how a cheat gets caught, in general terms: the slightest irregular action creates suspicion, "and mere suspicion will deplete the company". In other words, the great enemy of the card cheat is the watching eye of the other players.

Wait, really? Robert-Houdin noted that cheats could use a signalling code between partners "similar to that of my second sight", the verbal-code act he made famous on stage. The same idea can fool an audience in a theatre, or ruin an evening at a card table. This course keeps to the theatre.

title: The Man Who Fooled Houdini
description: Dai Vernon, the Ambitious Card, and a famous story told in several versions
tryIt: Practise the double lift ten times on its own, then perform the Ambitious Card first rise for one person, with a signed card.

concepts.title: How it works: a story told many ways
concepts.contentHtml:
David Frederick Wingfield Verner was born in Ottawa on 11 June 1894 and became Dai Vernon, "the Professor" of close-up card magic. He first read Erdnase as a boy: at 88 he was able to quote, from memory, a passage he had first read as a boy 80 years before.1 His reputation, though, rests on one night.

According to a 2006 profile in Magic magazine, on 6 February 1922 Vernon and a friend attended a banquet in honour of Harry Houdini in the Crystal Ballroom of the Great Northern Hotel in Chicago. Houdini had thrown down a challenge: he could not be fooled by a trick if he saw it three times in a row. Vernon performed the Ambitious Card, a signed card that keeps rising to the top of the deck however often it is buried, and fooled him not just once but eight times.2 From then on Vernon was billed as "the man who fooled Houdini".

How do we know? Only through the telling. The other account we read says Houdini watched seven times, and that his wife finally said "Face it, Houdini, you're fooled!" Nothing we found is a film or a transcript. The core is probably true: a young card man impressed the most famous magician alive, and made sure the world heard. The details are the sort that drift each time a story is told at a magicians' dinner.

Treat it as a lesson in method, not just in gossip. The trick Vernon used is not one new sleight but a plain, well-handled routine, which is exactly the skeleton you will learn next.

concepts.title: The method: the Ambitious Card, first rise
concepts.contentHtml:
In the Ambitious Card a signed card is lost in the middle of the deck and comes back to the top. Vernon's own version is far richer; this is the skeleton, using the double lift from Lifts and Forces. Example cards: Y is your crimped key (the 9♣) and X is their card (the Q♦).

  1. Set. Crimp the bottom card (Y) as in The Rising Card. They take any card, X, sign its face and lose it with the cut-and-cover, then cut as often as they like. Spread the deck, find the crimp and cut it to the top, flattening the curl. Y now lies over X, second from the top, and they never saw it go there.
  2. Show. Do the double lift: turn the top two cards over as one. They see X, signed. "Is this your card?"
  3. Turn back. Turn the pair face down again. The top card is Y, but they think it is X.
  4. Lose it. Take the top card (Y), push it into the middle of the deck and let them see it go in. "Your card is lost."
  5. Rise. Square up, snap your fingers and turn over the top card. It is the signed Q♦.

Why it works: the double lift shows the lower card of the pair, so what they see is X while what you push in is Y. The signature is your guarantee: the card they see twice carries the same mark. So far this is The Rising Card from Lifts and Forces with a signature added; Vernon's routine makes the card rise again and again, with more sleights between the rises, and the signature is what makes each rise impossible to explain away.

Common mistakes: letting the pair fall apart on the turn, hurrying the first display, and pushing the card in so fast they do not believe it is lost. Practise the double lift on its own until a single card and a double look the same on the table.

concepts.title: Myth check: the legend is not a record
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth The story of Vernon fooling Houdini is a fixed historical record.
Reality It is a legend that comes in several versions, so the number of repeats and the day you hear depend on who is telling it.

The profile in Magic says eight times; another account says that Houdini watched the trick seven times,1 each time asking for it to be repeated. Neither source offers a recording or a written note from Houdini. Both can fairly be called loyal tellings by Vernon's admirers. The honest summary is that Vernon impressed Houdini with a card trick at a Chicago banquet in the early 1920s, and Vernon made good use of it by billing himself as The Man Who Fooled Houdini.

Wait, really? The challenge itself is part of the story: that Houdini claimed he could not be fooled if allowed to see a trick three times. Magicians are used to that. A repeated trick is a hard test, because the audience can look harder each time. A good routine, like the Ambitious Card, is built so that watching harder does not help.

So when you perform it, do not promise a miracle. Ask them to watch closely, show the signature, and let the rising card do the talking. If the story of the night is a bit uncertain, the lesson is solid: the best card handling is the kind that looks like nothing.

title: From Card Table to Chalkboard
description: Persi Diaconis, magician turned mathematician, and a four-suit Gilbreath trick
tryIt: Set up the 16 cards and perform Four Suits in Every Four for one person, with the slip written before the shuffle.

concepts.title: How it works: a magician who became a professor
concepts.contentHtml:
Persi Diaconis was born in New York City in 1945 to professional musicians and studied the violin at Juilliard from the age of five to fourteen. He also taught himself magic tricks from the age of five. At 13 he met Martin Gardner, whose Scientific American column on mathematical games drew on ideas Diaconis showed him. Then, at fourteen, Dai Vernon invited Diaconis to join him on one of his American tours performing magic shows.1 Diaconis left school without telling his parents and went.

After a couple of years with Vernon he worked on his own, then went back to study. He took a degree in mathematics at the City College of New York in January 1971 and a PhD at Harvard in 1974, and that year became an assistant professor of statistics at Stanford, where he was a full professor by 1981.

The magic did not stop. In 1992 Dave Bayer and Diaconis published "Trailing the Dovetail Shuffle to its Lair", an analysis of the most commonly used way of shuffling cards. Its abstract says the result is a simple expression for the chance of any arrangement after any number of shuffles, and that Key ingredients are the analysis of a card trick and some deeper algebra. They found that \(\tfrac{3}{2}\log_2 n+\theta\) shuffles are necessary and sufficient to mix up \(n\) cards, so the number of shuffles needed grows only slowly as the deck gets bigger.

Diaconis is one of the clearest cases of a person who crossed from the card table to the chalkboard with the same questions: how many ways can a deck be ordered, and what do shuffles do to them?

concepts.title: The method: four suits in every four
concepts.contentHtml:
Many tricks in Diaconis and Ron Graham's book Magical Mathematics hang on one idea. Here is a four-suit version of the Gilbreath principle that you may have met with red and black cards. Use 16 cards: four of each suit, in any ranks.

  1. Set up. Arrange the 16 cards face down, top to bottom, in the repeating suit order club, heart, spade, diamond: ♣♥♠♦ four times. Write on a slip: "Every four cards will hold all four suits". Fold it and leave it where they can see it.
  2. Deal. Ask them to deal any number of cards from the top into a pile on the table, one at a time, face down. The pile is reversed.
  3. Riffle. Ask them to riffle that pile into the rest, once. It may be ragged; either side can drop first.
  4. Square. Pick up the deck without cutting or shuffling it. Say "that is as random as a shuffle gets".
  5. Reveal. Turn up the top four cards: one of each suit. Then the next four, and the next. Open the slip.

Why it works: the dealt pile counts the suit cycle backwards, the rest counts it forwards, and when four cards have come out of the riffle the two runs meet in the middle of the cycle. Together they cover four consecutive places, which are all four suits. Checked by computer for 16 and 52 cards over many random riffles, it never failed, provided there is just one riffle.

Mistakes: dealing the pile in a heap instead of one at a time, shuffling again, or cutting after the riffle. Any of these breaks the pattern.

concepts.title: Myth check: magic and maths are opposites
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Magic and mathematics are opposites: one is deception, the other truth.
Reality They overlap more than most people think; the Gilbreath principle is a card trick and it is also deep mathematics.

The St Andrews MacTutor biography of Diaconis reports that his book with Graham treats the Gilbreath principle, an effect where the cards stay in control despite being shuffled, as something that shares an intimate connection with the Mandelbrot set.1 The same biography says other tricks link to combinatorics, graph theory, number theory and topology.

That fits what you saw in the 1992 shuffle paper: the analysis of a card trick was a key ingredient of a result about how many shuffles it takes to mix a deck. A trick is a small experiment about how people and cards behave, and mathematicians like small experiments.

Wait, really? Diaconis did not come to mathematics through school success. He left high school early to tour with Vernon, and later got into Harvard with help from a letter by Martin Gardner. If you enjoy the four-suit trick, remember what it shows: you can build a deck that fools people from nothing more than a pattern and one honest riffle. The pattern does the work, and the performer's job is to make sure no one notices it.

title: The Deck in Your Head
description: Aronson and Tamariz's memorised decks, and a rule-based stack you can learn tonight
tryIt: Set up a Si Stebbins stack, practise Any Number in a Cut Deck until you can name the card in under five seconds, then perform it for one person.

concepts.title: How it works: a deck you carry in your head
concepts.contentHtml:
A memorised deck is a pack whose order you know by heart. Name any card and you can say where it is; name any position and you can say which card sits there. Magicians call a known order a stack. Cut the deck, and a cyclic stack survives, because (as in the first lesson of the Key Card skill) a cut only decides where the ring is opened.

It is a young craft in print. A 2004 review on a magic dealer's blog says Simon Aronson was beginning to publish stack material1 in April 1973 in a one-man issue of Kabbala, followed by tricks in Card Ideas of Simon Aronson in 1978 and his own stack in the 1979 pamphlet A Stack to Remember. The same review says that in 2000, at the FISM convention in Portugal, Juan Tamariz released a two-volume set of books,2 Sinfonia en Mnemonica Mayor ("Symphony in Mnemonic Major"), later combined into one volume in English by Hermetic Press. It describes the stack known as Mnemonica.

The full Mnemonica order is the property of that book, so this course does not reprint it. What you can learn is the principle behind every memorised deck: store the order in your head so well that you can work with it at conversation speed.

That is where the Memory Palace course comes in. Its deck skill, beginning with "The Whole Routine", shows how to turn 52 cards into images and walk them through a palace in order. A magician uses the same tools, then performs from the stack instead of reciting it to a stopwatch. Memory sport asks "how fast can you learn a random deck?". Magic asks "what can I do once I know it?".

concepts.title: The method: any number in a cut deck
concepts.contentHtml:
Learning a random order is a big job. A Si Stebbins stack is a shortcut: the order follows a rule, so you remember the rule and not 52 cards. Each card is three higher than the one before (counting K, then A, 2, 3, round the ring) and the suits repeat in the order club, heart, spade, diamond. Top to bottom, face down, it starts: A♣ 4♥ 7♠ 10♦ K♣ 3♥ 6♠ 9♦ Q♣ 2♥ 5♠ 8♦ J♣ A♥ 4♠ 7♦ and carries on to the 52nd card.

  1. Set. Lay the stack out beforehand using the rule. Check card 14 is the A♥.
  2. Cut. Let them cut the deck as often as they like, completing each cut. Never shuffle.
  3. Glimpse. Square the deck and read the bottom card. (Example: the 9♦.)
  4. Number. Ask them to think of any number from 1 to 13. Say 7.
  5. Work it out. The top card is one step on from the bottom card, so the 7th card is seven steps on. Add 3 times n to the value (counting round the ring) and move the suit on n places.
  6. Name it. Say "the four of spades". Have them deal seven cards face down and turn the seventh over.

Shortcut for the values: for n = 1 to 13, the amount to add is 3, 6, 9, −1, 2, 5, 8, −2, 1, 4, 7, −3, 0. The suit moves n places round club, heart, spade, diamond, so only the remainder of n over 4 matters.

Worked check: 9 + 8 = 17, which is 4 once you go round the ring of 13, and 7 places from ♦ is 3 places, which is ♠. Mistakes: letting a spectator riffle the deck, counting the bottom card as card 1 and forgetting that the top card is the first step on.

concepts.title: Myth check: everyone spots a stack
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Anyone watching a memorised-deck routine can tell the deck is stacked.
Reality Even at a convention of magicians, a reviewer recalls that only a few recognised the stack.

The review of Tamariz's book recalls seeing him perform a routine from Mnemonica at a close-up convention in 1990, and says: "Despite the sophisticated company at the 4F gathering, I believe only a few recognized that the method was in fact a stack1". The reviewer adds that the memorised deck is "the defining trend of fin de siecle card magic". A routine can look like a free choice or a coincidence, when the performer knows exactly where every card is.

That is not a licence to be careless. Keep the pattern out of sight, let them cut but never shuffle, and keep the story plain and truthful, as Robert-Houdin did: you are playing a person who has practised.

Wait, really? Cyclic stacks do not need to be learned as 52 separate cards. If you can say "add three, next suit", you hold the entire order in your head by arithmetic. Combine that with a Memory Palace and you can do both: arithmetic for a quick party piece, images for a fully random order.

You have now met a gentleman conjuror, a book with no author, a legendary banquet, a professor who began as a card man and a deck that lives in the head. Your last test is to choose one of these tricks and perform it for a real person, in your own character, with a straight face.
